title: What they're saying before Michigan football vs. Iowa - NewsBreak
text:
By Clayton Sayfie ,
21 hours ago
Michigan Wolverines football head coach Kyle Whittingham during a win over Western Michigan in 2026. (Photo by IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect) Michigan Wolverines football is set to take on Iowa Saturday in Ann Arbor. Here’s a look around the internet at what they’re saying before kickoff.
Tom Kakert, Hawkeye Report: Game Preview: Iowa at Michigan Iowa hits the road for the first time in the 2026 season. This is a younger Iowa team and it’s also one where there will be a large chunk of the starters making their first start on the road. And that first start is going to be in front of 107,000 fans in Ann Arbor.
That means the start to this game will be important for the Hawkeye. They need to avoid the big mistake that could prove to be costly in what I think will be a low scoring contest.
The keys to this one are very simple. I think whoever wins the turnover battle will win the game. I want to see how Hank Brown and the Iowa offense handles being in a hostile atmosphere. Will they be able to take care of the football? After struggling to run the football against Iowa State and their aggressive defense, will Iowa be able to run the ball against Michigan’s aggressive attack on defense?
From the Michigan perspective, other than a second half outburst against a bad UTEP team, Michigan’s offense has not been great. Can Bryce Underwood make plays in the passing game? Will Iowa be able to slow him down when he decides to run the ball?
Basically, I think this is a game that will be low scoring and turnovers will be critical. I think this one just slips away from the Hawkeyes. MICHIGAN 17 IOWA 13. My pick to click is Tony Diaz, who has one touchdown reception.
Richard Johnson, CBS Sports: Inside Bryce Underwood’s evolution: Michigan QB coach details development into pocket passer For Underwood, as it is with many quarterbacks, inaccuracy starts with footwork. A key play happened in that Western Michigan game. On an early third down in the second quarter, Underwood missed a wide-open running back in the flat for what would have been an easy first down. It’s the little things that Michigan is trying to get him to refine as a passer. Much has been made of Underwood not having a true quarterback coach in Year 1 under Sherrone Moore. When Detmer first got Underwood, they leaned into his strengths throwing outside the pocket on the move. During spring and summer, the focus shifted to developing his game inside the pocket.
“Whenever there is any inaccuracy, I think it always starts from the ground up, and I think sometimes whether it be alignment, feet, shoulders, whatever that case may be, is where he can sometimes maybe be a little bit off, and we always try to, in practice, try to make everything as stressful as possible, specifically with the pocket and everything that we’re doing individual-wise,” Detmer said. “Because sometimes you can kind of feel that rush or feel that pocket collapsing on your feet, where now maybe you’re not able to get into your throw. And I think that’s sometimes where the inaccuracies come from. And so just continuing every day, in individual and in practice, as much as we can, create those kind of tougher situations around the pocket, so that then when we get into game, then we’re better stepping our throw, being aligned, and those sort of things.”
Manny Navarro, The Athletic: Is Sam Leavitt’s accuracy a problem? Is Oregon still a title contender? Week 4 panic meter 7. Can Michigan win big without a dependable passing game? Michigan is unbeaten despite having an anemic passing attack that ranks 109th nationally with 175.7 yards per game.
Bryce Underwood needed a controversial last-second Hail Mary to rescue the Wolverines against Western Michigan, and he threw for just 111 yards in a 17-10 win at home against Oklahoma. His legs are an asset, but they shouldn’t have to be the answer whenever the passing game stalls.
Saturday’s win over UTEP provided encouraging signs: Underwood completed 19 of 25 passes for 223 yards and two touchdowns. The question is whether that improvement carries over to conference play, which begins this week against Iowa.
Michigan has generated only seven explosive plays of 20-plus yards, tied with Michigan State and Texas A&M for the fewest among P4 programs.
A defense allowing 3.8 yards per play gives Underwood room to develop. But eventually, somebody will make Michigan chase instead of protecting a lead. The Wolverines need Underwood’s recent passing performance to become the expectation, not the exception.
Panic meter: 5
Joel Klatt, Fox Sports: Will Ole Miss Extend Streak? Can USC Top Oregon? Joel Klatt’s Week 4 CFB Picks The winner of this game is set up for … this just feels like a low-scoring slug fest. Doesn’t it? It’s got to. Both defenses are very good, although they do it different ways, schematically. It’s hard for me to see how Iowa is going to throw the ball in this game. We saw how good Michigan’s defense can be, namely in that Oklahoma game … Can Iowa throw the football? I want you to pay attention to the tight end for Iowa. Because that’s the best matchup you are looking at the Michigan defense, I think it will be almost impossible to throw against those corners, they play with three of them.
If you’re looking for the ways Iowa can not just run the football to succeed, but get the ball down the field, I think it’s got to be the tight end. The tight end matchup. Now for the Michigan offense, I think this is a really bad matchup for the Michigan offense.
I think Michigan wins 13-10, but Iowa takes the 4.5.
Klatt’s straight-up pick: Michigan
Klatt’s pick against the spread: Iowa +5.5
Scott Dochterman, The Athletic: Who belongs on the Big Ten’s CFP bubble? Week 4 will speak volumes about contenders Those six teams are on the periphery of the CFP discussion. And with a loss, their chances of re-entering that conversation fall significantly.
According to projections from The Athletic ’s Austin Mock , those teams’ CFP chances drop by at least half with a loss this week. In particular, the loser of Iowa-Michigan has only a 3 percent chance of reaching the CFP, according to Mock’s model. For a sport where reaching the 12-team CFP has become the only goal, it puts a ton of pressure on a single game in late September.
“As soon as we went to four (CFP teams in 2014), I think that was the beginning of not only the erosion of the bowl system, but maybe the end here in the near … at least it’s going to look different than it used to,” Iowa coach Kirk Ferentz said. “It already does. It’s just the world we’ve created, and you deal with it. But I try not to let that worry me too much and just worry about enjoying our players and getting ready for the next challenge, which right now is a significant one.”
The CFP paths for Iowa and Michigan, both 3-0, are vastly different, which makes their first matchup in Ann Arbor since 2019 even more important.
Austin Meek, The Athletic: Is Michigan vs. Iowa first to 10 points wins? 3 big questions and a prediction I picked Iowa to win this game before the season, and nothing I’ve seen compels me to change the prediction. The Hawkeyes got all they could handle from a rebuilding Iowa State team, but that’s typical for the Cy-Hawk rivalry. They’ve looked impressive in their other games — especially last week, when they ran for 422 yards with three 100-yard rushers.
Michigan’s defense has been very good, but Oklahoma doesn’t have much of a run game and scored 14 points against New Mexico a week after scoring 10 in Ann Arbor. Western Michigan might be the best offense Michigan has faced to this point, and the Broncos had success controlling the ball, just as Iowa will try to do. This could be the week when Michigan’s offensive limitations finally catch up with the Wolverines.
Prediction: Iowa 21, Michigan 16
